utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Before we hear the witness, I think there are a few words that I would like to say to the parties. We have gone through two witnesses this week and we are not that satisfied with the proceedings, because we found that the scope is too broad and some questions, both in direct examination and cross-examination, are not so closely related to the actual conduct of the accused, Mr. Jokic. So I hope that in future proceedings, both parties should be more concentrated on the subject matter of this case. We have heard a lot about the atrocities that happened during that period, the fighting situations, but the main purpose of this hearing is to see whether Mr. Jokic is innocent or not. I hope both parties could bear that in mind, and we have to finish the hearings of this case before the summer recess. Yes, Mr. Stojanovic, any protective measures for the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. No protective measures have been asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Can we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper Madam Usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Stojanovic, the witness is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please tell us your full name.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Ljubo Bojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: For the record, please spell your name.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: L-j-u-b-o B-o-j-a-n-o-v-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bojanovic, when were you born and where?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 9th of August, 1947, in Sarajevo, Centre municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you spend your childhood, Mr. Bojanovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: From the age of 5, I have lived in Zvornik, which means that after the first five years in Sarajevo our family moved to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What was the reason for their move from Sarajevo to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The climate did not suit my late father, and my family moved to Zvornik. And both my parents come originally from a place near Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you finish your primary and secondary school there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Zvornik. I graduated from the primary school and the secondary school before enrolling in the military academy in 1966, which I completed in 1970. It was the academy of the ground forces, artillery section.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Upon completion of your military education, were you trained and qualified and took up an active military job?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, after graduating from the academy, I received what we call a transfer in the army to a place called Krusevac in Serbia. I spent four years there before spending another two years in Aleksinac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where is the town of Aleksinac located?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It is along the Belgrade/Nis highway, about 30 kilometres from Nis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How long did you serve in the army professionally?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Until the 31st of December, 1975.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you leave the army then?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on my own initiative because I did not like the military lifestyle. It did not suit my ambitions and I didn't see any prospects or promising future for myself in the army, so I returned to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When did you come back to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the beginning of 1976.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you find a job in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Since my former teacher was the director of the military training centre, his name was Vojin Pasic [phoen], he involved me in the process of teaching All People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of subject is that? What did you teach the children?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That subject had an educational and upbringing aspect. I familiarised children with the basic characteristics of the most common weapons which were not the most modern ones. Many lessons had to do with measures of civilian defence so that children should know what to do in case of earthquake, floods, fires, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How long did you remain a teacher?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I worked in this technical training centre for over 16 years, and that's where the war found me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember what rank you held at the outbreak of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I held the rank of captain first class, and I was assigned to the Territorial Defence of the Zvornik municipality. It was the broader area of Tuzla Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when the Zvornik Brigade was established.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At the outset, there was a headquarters of Territorial Defence, and people joined in. It was not a real army or a formally established brigade at the beginning. The brigade was set up in the middle of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When the Zvornik Brigade was formed, did you join in?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was mobilised into those forces that existed then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, Mr. Bojanovic, what duties did you perform in the Zvornik Brigade in those first days.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During those first days, I was at Alhos, which was in fact a factory whose premises we used as headquarters for the Territorial Defence. Things were not completely organised then, and my duties were not strictly and clearly defined.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How did things develop in terms of your wartime assignment and the duties you performed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: After the fall of Kula town, which is a hill above -- overlooking Zvornik, I was assigned to be commander of a reinforced company over there, where I stayed until September 1992 as the main commanding officer on that elevation which had great strategic importance for the town of Zvornik and Podrinje, the Drina valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: After that, where were you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: After that, I went back to the brigade performing operative duties, standing duty guard, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us more precisely when did you practically move to the operations section of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Immediately after I left Kula Grad where I handed over to someone else my unit of the 6th Battalion, and I believe it was in October 1992. I started working then in what was later to become the operations organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In end-1992, who was the commander of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pandurevic arrived around the 17th of December to the command post then located in Orahovac. I know this because he arrived the day before my patron saint's day, which is St. Nicholas.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who was chief of staff then?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Major Obrenovic. He could have been captain then. You will excuse me if I don't remember all the ranks people held at that time, but I believe he was captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Until when did you stay in the operations organ of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I think until March 1993, when the then-major Pandurevic appointed him -- appointed me assistant commander for morale and religion -- correction, religion and legal affairs. I remained on that post until end-1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: After being assistant commander for morale until end-1993, where did you transfer?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I transferred, according to the needs of the service, to the operations organ. I was a trained officer and I was qualified.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How long did you remain in the operations organ of the Zvornik Brigade in that second round, that second stint?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Until the beginning of July 1995, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What happened in the beginning of July 1995 in terms of your functional duties?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Again, to meet the needs of the service and on the verbal orders of the commander, I transferred to the service for morale, religious, and legal affairs. There was not enough qualified personnel in that organ, and somebody needed to help out. My commanding officer was Major Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: For the record, tell us the name of Major Simic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Major Nenad Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So, from the first half of July until when did you remain in the section for morale of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe I stayed there until the completion of all combat activities, until the signing of the Dayton Accords, with the proviso that I did other jobs and perform other duties that are not strictly under the purview of this section for morale, religious, and legal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At this point, I wanted to ask you how long have you known Dragan Jokic. When did you first meet him?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I have known him since he was a boy, because we lived next door. There were about 50 metres between our houses. I am 10 years his senior so we didn't socialise much, but I saw him around.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see him again when the war started?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I met up with him again when he came to be the chief of that formation, which was to become the Zvornik Brigade, and he came to inspect my unit at Kula Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How long did he remain chief of staff in the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember the exact time, but I know it was not long. We did not keep in touch. I was far away from the headquarters, from the command, so I don't really know when he stopped being chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what position was assigned to him after that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you, I can't be sure because I wasn't kept posted. I think he transferred to the Army of Yugoslavia, but he was absent for a very short time. And when he came back again, he was appointed chief of engineers in the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Allow me, Mr. Bojanovic, to take you back again to year 1995 so that you explain to us the positions and the structure within the Zvornik Brigade. Can you remember in July 1995 who was commander of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In July, brigade commander was the then-Lieutenant Colonel Vinko Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who was chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Major Dragan Obrenovic was the chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And what about the hierarchical structure of the Zvornik Brigade and its command. What did the rest of it look like?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to commander and chief of staff, the command also included assistant commander for logistics, assistant commander for security, and assistant commander for morale, religious, and legal affairs. Therefore, the five of them comprised the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who held the post of the assistant commander for logistics?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Assistant commander for logistics was the then-Captain Sreten Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What about assistant commander for security?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That post was held by Lieutenant Drago Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that command is comprised of these five people, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, commander, with the rest of the command, plans the activities of the brigade, all of the activities, which means that these people are his direct assistants.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So the members of this inner command, as you call them, are they hierarchically above the rest of the staff officers?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Following the commander of the chief of staff, we have the three assistants and then the rest of the staff officers. This is the military hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the command of the Zvornik Brigade have a staff as an organised structure?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a staff and Major Dragan Obrenovic held the post of the chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who was in the staff of the Zvornik Brigade? Who were the staff officers?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the chief of staff, the officers who were directly subordinated to him were assistant to the chief of staff for training and operation -- operative affairs. Then assistant chief of staff for intelligence and reconnaissance, and assistant chief of staff for personnel, and chiefs of arms of service that existed in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us who held which posts in the staff of the Zvornik Brigade. Who was the assistant chief of staff for operative affairs and training?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That post was held by Major Miodrag Dragutinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who was the assistant chief of staff for intelligence?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The assistant chief of staff for intelligence was Captain Dusan or Dusko Vukotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And who was assistant chief of staff for personnel and general administration?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That post of the assistant chief of staff for personnel and general administration was held by Milan Galic, who was a major.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you serve at the time, in what organ, in the beginning of July?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the beginning of July up until the 8th of July, I served in the operations organ. And then on the 8th or maybe the 9th, pursuant to a verbal order of the commander, I was transferred to the organ for morale.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Up until your transfer, who served in the training and operative affairs organ of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That is one of the most important organs, and up until that time there were five or six senior officers, first class captains or majors, serving in that organ. And if you wish, I can give you their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please. Could you tell us the names of these officers?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stojanovic, I don't think there's any disputes about the structure and the commanders in those structures. Could we go over this section as soon as possible? Unless you believe some information is very closely related to your client.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honour, I do take into account all of your suggestions, also the ones that you gave before this examination-in-chief. But due to the fact that one segment of the indictment speaks about the position held by Mr. Jokic, we wanted to explain all of the positions that existed in the staff and who held those posts. So we will try to cover this very briefly so as not to spend too much time on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed. But please bear in mind our concerns in this aspect. And we also believe that we have a kind of chart of the structures of the brigade. Maybe we could use it to see where your client fit in.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I think we have used this organogramme a number of times, but because of that organogramme which shows all staff officers as being on the same level, we wanted to show exactly what were the authorities and tasks and duties of all of those officers. Thank you again, and we will not dwell on this for too long.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bojanovic, at one point you said that the operative organ was the soul of the staff or something along those lines. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, all of the activities in the brigade go through that organ, starting with the training, the control over the units, and all other affairs that are of importance for the life of the unit, especially if there are any combat operations. Those were the times when this organ was activated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that that organ had personnel of sufficient quality and number at the time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said that in addition to assistant chief of staff for personnel, there were some three or four majors in that organ and two captains who also had some pre-war experience with that area of expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the decision-making process and consultations with the chief of staff, would these three assistant chiefs of staff for personnel, intelligence, and operative affairs and training, would they be above other senior officers?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, definitely. Especially the assistant chief of staff for operative affairs and training.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And this is why I wanted now to turn to the position of the chief of arms of service. Can you tell us how many assistant chiefs of arms of service there were?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Major Dragan Jokic was in charge of engineering; Milisav Petrovic, a captain, was in charge of communications; chief of artillery was Captain or Major Miodrag Maksimovic; chief of air defence and air force affairs was a man whose name I cannot recall now. So these are mostly the people that I can recall now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What were the duties of the chiefs of arms of service in the staff of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The chiefs of arms of service, regardless of what service it was, served as advisors, because they were experts in their field. They were in the position to propose to command through the chief of staff how to use the units of their arms of service in special type of combat action and so on, or they would propose something regarding what their unit could do. So they had this role of advisors. And they were liaisons between the chief of staff and the units within their arms of service.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time in July of 1995, did the Zvornik Brigade have an engineering company within its structure?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At the time and also before, they had an engineering company which was some 2 kilometres from the command at another location near Omladinsko Naselje settlement. This company had its commander and its own structure with three platoons I think. They also had certain equipment belonging to the company.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What were the duties and tasks of the engineering company within the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, analysing the structure of the engineering company, which had the so-called pioneering platoon and also construction platoon and machinery platoon, one can conclude what were the duties of the engineering company, to put up blockades, to build fortifications, to transport something, to do all the jobs that required the use of machinery, construction machinery.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What were the duties of this pioneering platoon, as you called it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The pioneering platoon built obstacles using mines and explosives, and also other kinds of obstacles.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Bojanovic, whether battalions within the Zvornik Brigade also had soldiers who were skilled in engineering activities?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Each battalion had three or four so-called engineers so that they could use them in the areas of defence of their battalions to build these obstacles using mines and explosives and so on. The chief of staff was responsible for their training.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The chief of arms of service, was he able to issue any orders or to command the engineering company? Here I'm referring to chief of engineering service.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Chief of engineering service was unable to issue direct orders to commanders of those units.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the principle of the unity of command, who was in command of the engineering company?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The engineering company and other units within various arms of service were under the command of commanders of those units because if it weren't structured in that way, then what other role would the commander of a unit play.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could the commander of an engineering company on his own without prior consent of the chief of staff use the engineering company as he sees fit?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. Under no circumstances can he use the troops or the machinery without prior consent of the commander of the brigade or chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And in that system of the unity of command and subordination, what is the role of the chief of arms of service in addition to this advisory role that he plays, what other duties and tasks would that person perform?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the chief of arms of service has a role of training of, let's say, engineering unit or any other unit, so they are in charge of training, they propose personnel to fill certain positions, they are in charge of equipment for their unit, and that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In July of 1995, were these principles applied in the functioning of the staff of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. These principles were applied then and prior to the events of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "functioning," do you mean to say that the military rules and the military discipline were upheld in the staff of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, naturally. That's how I see it and that's how I described it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like now to ask you a few things about your position. What was the reason for your transfer to the organ for morale from the operative organ?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The reason for my transfer - and I was transferred pursuant to the order of the commander - was that the organ for morale had only assistant commander. It did not have any other senior officers who could carry out the duties, and there were a lot of duties and a lot of work. And since I already had some experience in that area, I was the most proper person to fill that post.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In those days when you worked in the organ for morale, what were your duties and tasks?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My job was first and foremost to carry out the orders of the assistant commander for morale. His orders mostly pertained to organisations of funerals, and there were a lot of them at the time, to ensure that we had everything needed for the funeral, and also to inform the family of the soldier who had been killed, which was a thankless task as you can see. Then we had to organise funerals, arrange for the speeches and so on. Sometimes he was involved in that and sometimes I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did somebody stand in for you in the operative organ during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. Nobody stood in for me because there were no people, and despite having been transferred to the organ for morale I also performed duties of the duty operations officer, which means that I continued performing some other duties that had nothing to do with morale. But we simply did not have enough people, so I had to carry on with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, briefly what were the duties of the security organ and what authority did that organ of the Zvornik Brigade have.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I can tell you what my view is. The security organ was in charge of security in the area of defence of the Zvornik Brigade. And it cooperated with the organs of the MUP. I never went into any deeper analysis of the work of those organs, because in a way I was intimidated by them. I used to serve in the former JNA, and these security organs then and later on in Republika Srpska as well were always separate in a way there. Their senior officers had special authorities. Commander of the unit even didn't have to be informed about all of their activities. They had their own separate hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What were the authorities of Drago Nikolic at the time, who was assistant commander in that field?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if I could I would call him grey eminence. He was a person who dealt with the commander and probably conveyed to him the information that he wanted to convey.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that due to such treatment of the security organ in the Zvornik Brigade, there was some problems between Pandurevic and Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was present as duty operations officer when a telegram arrived from the Main Staff, and Drago Nikolic and his people complained in that telegram that the commander was interfering in their affairs. The telegram stated that they should straighten out their relations and that the security organ should carry on with its duties and tasks without much involvement on the part of the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bojanovic, if I may ask you to cam back to the position of the chief of engineers, what was the personality of Dragan Jokic and what was his influence in decision-making overall within such a structure of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I can say that he was neglected, especially in the distribution of roles. And in many cases he was underestimated, both by the chief of staff and the commander of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On what do you base this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Probably due to the overall relations, as they were. Major Jokic seemed to lose all ambition and couldn't wait for the war to end. That was in stark contrast to Pandurevic and the other senior officers who were ambitious and aspired to military careers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did he play an active part? Did he have a prominent role in the work of the staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: He executed his tasks and he tried as hard as he could; however, his performance was not properly valued. I remember certain meetings held in a broader composition, including the top command and the lower officers, where critique was addressed to Major Jokic whether he had performed well or poorly. He always seemed to be the target of criticism.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: To what extent did chief of staff Obrenovic appreciate his position, his rank, and himself as a person?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This does not apply to Major Jokic alone but to other commanding officers as well. He did not really value his qualifications, his performance, and his work.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that there were personal problems between Obrenovic and Jokic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: There were. The situation itself where Jokic was senior in age and in rank found himself subordinated to the younger chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it the case that even then in July 1995, if you can remember, there was a discrepancy, a difference, in rank between Jokic and Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: With the leave of this Honourable Court and with your permission, I would like to explain a couple of things. I won't take long. I met Mr. Pandurevic as captain first class. Eight or nine years later, he was promoted four steps up the ladder and he was a major. I met Jokic as --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the ranks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both of them were promoted four ranks up. Major Jokic received two ranks only, I believe, after one year. So these two ambitious senior officers, Pandurevic and Obrenovic, were promoted four ranks in that time. One of them emerging as a major general, and another one as lieutenant colonel. Whereas, Jokic was promoted only two ranks, which means that the two of them only executed the orders of the superior commanders and required their subordinates to carry out their own orders unquestioningly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bojanovic, could we stop here for a moment for the sake of the interpreters and repeat these ranks. After the end of the war you said that Vinko Pandurevic had which rank?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Major general. He received it in 1999 or 2000, but in any case he was a major general. And he was assistant chief of Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And which rank did Dragan Obrenovic hold after the war?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant colonel, whereas the first time I met him he was 2nd lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me just ask you one more thing. Within the structure of the Zvornik Brigade, as it was, who issued orders to subordinated units? Who was the one with the power to use any unit whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was within the discretion and the power of a unit commander to issue orders to a particular unit, but with the consent of the chief of staff or the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was it possible at any time for a chief of an arm of service without the knowledge or consent of the commander or the chief of staff to issue orders to a unit, to command a unit or tell them what to do.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That was not possible. There was always the commander of the unit or the chief of staff or the brigade commander who were there to issue orders. The chief of an arm of service could not directly command units.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it possible for a chief of an arm of service to bypass the chief of staff or the commander and send a unit to the defence area of another brigade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. That is not possible. That situation could not occur. He could not use that unit before consulting the chief of staff or the commander in getting their approval, and least of all was he able to command the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does every and any use of a unit imply the consumption of materiel such as ammunition, food, fuel, and would the organ for logistics supply such materiel without the knowledge of the chief of staff or the commander?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It is quite normal that a lot of materiel, especially in the case of engineers, is used in such activities, such as fuel, food, machinery, et cetera, but all this was settled through the assistant commander for logistics, even the chief of staff alone could not handle that himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Since we are interested, Mr. Bojanovic, in the period of July 1995, could you tell us: In those days, in the first half of July, where was Vinko Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Vinko Pandurevic, as brigade command, left accompanied by a part of mostly elite units of the Zvornik Brigade to be in the field and to deal with Srebrenica and Zepa, to work on Srebrenica and Zepa as we used to say in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In that period when Pandurevic was absent from the defence area of the Zvornik Brigade, who was in command of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant colonel chief of staff Dragan Obrenovic, who was his deputy automatically within that structure, was in charge. Either in writing or verbally he was put in charge in the absence of the commander, because ex officio he is the deputy of the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Bojanovic, if any oral or verbal -- or written orders existed on this transfer of authority from Pandurevic to Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any written order because I was in the organ for morale. If I had been part of the organ for operations, I would have certainly known of the existence of such a paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This begs the question: Did Obrenovic really de facto discharge the duties of the commander?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: De facto, he was the only one in the absence of the commander issuing orders that had to be executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to move very quickly through the couple of days that preceded the critical events, concentrating on the duties of the duty operations officer. Mr. Bojanovic, can you remember the day of the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I can. It was on the 11th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How did you find out about the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I learnt about it at the command, at the headquarters of the brigade. You find out immediately through our communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you spend the night of the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe on the 11th, 12th, 13th, and 14th I was certainly at the barracks, at the headquarters. When I say "the barracks" and "the headquarters," I mean one and the same thing. I was performing the duties assigned to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who was the duty operations officer on the 11th of July at the brigade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember. I don't have the list, the schedule, in front of me. I don't have the roster with me, so I can't say. It could have been me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And how about the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was again at the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember what were you doing on that day at the barracks?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the 12th of July? I think I was following the orders of Major Nenad Simic regarding affairs in the area of morale, dealing with those funerals. I can't remember exactly what I was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember who was the duty operations officer on the 12th of July at the brigade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was Major Maric who was captain at the time, although again I'm not sure about the ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During those days, did you see Dragan Obrenovic at the brigade? Was he performing his duties?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean this period, the 11th and 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not see him in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Whose instructions did you follow at the time in your work?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I followed the instructions of my superior officer, Major Nenad Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, by the way, Mr. Bojanovic, were you ever in a position to be the duty operations officer?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that out of all the commanding officers of my rank, I spent the most time working as the duty operations officer during the war and later. On one occasion even -- in fact, for a while even I was head of the operations team, which included five or six commanding officers, and we organised operations, duty service, to make it function as well as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What do you think was the reason why you happened to be the duty operations officer of the brigade so often?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The reason must have been that I had a lot of experience in these military affairs and that from the beginning of combat operations and the establishment of the brigade I was frequently in that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In principle, is it the case that it was the security organs who provided duty operations officers?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: According to the instructions on their work, they were given approval not to serve as duty operations officers because they had a similar duty in their own security organs. All the others were from time to time assigned to serve as duty operations officer, depending on the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the schedule of the shifts of the duty operations officer, was that something that was determined in advance?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Before the 1st of every month, the list would be published for the next month of duty operations officer by dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who made this roster?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This roster was made by someone in the operations organ, whether it was the assistant chief of staff or somebody authorised by the chief. And this list, depending on the situation, sometimes the list would not be adhered to because some officer had some other duties for that certain day and then he would be replaced by someone else. But this would only happen amongst those who were already on the list for the shifts as duty operations officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How long did a shift last of a duty operations officer in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The shift would last 24 hours. It would be the duty operations officer and his assistant. This was a very difficult and responsible job where people get tired very easily and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could the duty operations officers leave their post?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Only in exceptional circumstances could they leave their post to carry out another task, but then the office would be manned by the assistant or by someone else who was acting as a duty operations officer, somebody who was already on the list. A young soldier could not substitute for somebody who was trained and authorised to perform this function.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what the job was of the assistant of the duty operations officer.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: His duty would be in case of absence, to stand in for the duty operations officer. And it was also his duty to be on-call or to substitute for the duty operations officer during the 24-hour shift while the duty operations officer was resting or was absent for a little while, for as long as the shift lasted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean at a certain point when the duty operations officer was resting or left the room the assistant would take over the tasks of a duty operations officer?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, as well as while the duty operations officer was doing his shift, the assistant would also be involved in conveying all the orders, messages, and so on to those they were addressed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In Zvornik Brigade, where was the duty operations officer physically while performing his tasks?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In my interview on the 18th of September, 2001, I drew a kind of diagram where this office was. The office was facing the river Drina. That's where the duty operations officer's room was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was this office in the Standard building?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The building was actually intended to be used as a shoe factory but it never actually started to operate. So prior to the commencement of combat operations, it was turned into the command for the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The duty operations officer's room, was it secured? Was access forbidden to others? Or was it just like any other office?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As a rule, the duty operations officer and his assistant were not supposed to leave that room for 24 hours nor were others supposed to enter that room, except for the commander, the chief of staff, or the security organ members. Sometimes, though, somebody would enter to ask for information. Also, that was the only room that had a television in the entire command. So sometimes when there was some special programme or a soccer match or something, the commander would permit others to come into the room so that they could watch the programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us how the handover of duty between the outgoing and incoming duty operations officer was carried out, how was the notebook passed on and so on. Could you tell us briefly.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: For example, if I was the duty operations officer, my successor would come half an hour before his shift began. The changeover usually took place between 8.30 and 9.00. He would come in a half-hour before his shift was to begin. I would acquaint him with the working tasks and the duties that were ahead of him, those that were underway or should be implemented. We would both sign my remarks or entries that I made during my shift, both of us would sign this. And then when all the documents were prepared, we would then go either to see the commander. If he was absent, we would then go to the chief of staff and that's where the transfer of the shift would be completed. During the handover, the outgoing person would pass over the tasks to the incoming person. And then the outgoing and the incoming duty operations officers would sign the logbook.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more question, Your Honours, and then I think it will be time for the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the handover of duty could not be carried out without the permission and signature of the chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's how it was in principle. Sometimes it would happen that neither of the commander or the chief of staff were absent, neither of them were there. And then they would tell us, well, you hand over the shift and then when we come back then we will sign the appropriate book and issue the tasks for the incoming duty operations officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps this would be a convenient time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll take a break. We'll resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic, I believe that you made some progress compared with yesterday, but still there is some room for improvement. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Every day in every way, I am improving. And let's hope that this will continue to go on like that. I would just like to ask the usher for her assistance to give the witness the excerpt from the manual for the operations of staffs and commands. This is Exhibit P394 and is a part of Mr. Richard Butler's report. It's a document that we used when we examined the witness yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bojanovic, may we continue?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at Article 66 about -- from the manual, which regulates the duties of the duty operations officer. And could you please answer a question that is crucial in our defence and that is: Which are the tasks, the duties, the obligations of the duty operations officer?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The duties of the duty operations officer is to follow the course of combat operations and to look at the working maps, to enter the changes with their own and neighbouring units. Do I need to repeat my answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If you can just read a little bit more slowly, Mr. Bojanovic, because of the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This is because I am repeating. Then, "to inform the commander or the chief of staff about any major changes or orders issued by a superior which require a decision of the commander; to be familiar with the disposition of elements of the command post, the location of the commander, chief of staff, and assistants to the commander; to control and maintain communications with the operations duty officers of the superior and subordinate commands."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we just focus on this for a moment. How do you comment and interpret this task, in view of the fact that you were a duty operations officer? What is actually the task of the duty operations officer?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Even though these duties have been copied from the rules of service of the former JNA, the task, as it is here, is to -- for the duty operations officer to transfer orders from superior to the lower command, from the corps commander to the brigade commander, and to the subordinate units, and the other way around, from the bottom to the top. So his task is to convey information. The duty operations officer is a form of relay, a medium for the transfer of information, orders, and instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain this to us using practical examples.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: For example, regardless of the kind of order, the duty operations officer does not have to deal with the essence or the substance of that order but just needs to convey it to the officer who is supposed to receive this order. And also, it works from the bottom upwards. The operations officer does not need to know what the essence is or the substance of the order but just needs to transfer it to the right person.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Hypothetically speaking, in practice we can have the following situation: The commander of the Drina Corps or the commander of the brigade requests that the duty operations officer conveys an order to the 1st Battalion of the Zvornik Brigade to send 40 soldiers to the Snagovo sector. What is the duty of the duty operations officer when he receives such an order?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It is his duty to call the duty operations officer of the battalion or the unit and to convey to him the orders from the corps command or from the chief of staff or from the commander. He only has to convey this to the other operations officer. And then it is his duty in turn to inform his commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is the commander duty-bound to tell the duty operations officer the content of the order and -- or the reasons for a decision? Is he obliged to tell the duty operations officer why he requires 40 soldiers at Snagovo?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, he's not duty-bound or obliged to do that. It is only the duty of the operations officer to convey such an order, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Another example: The chief of staff or the brigade commander asks the duty operations officer to send machinery from the engineering company to the Orahovac sector. Is the commander obliged to tell the duty operations officer why these machines are required to be sent there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I repeat once again that he is not obliged to tell that to the duty operations officer. The duty operations officer does not need to know why the machinery is required.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I will try to turn this question around. Is the duty operations officer obliged or does he have the right to ask the commander why these machines need to go to that sector?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That was never the practice of the duty operations officer. It is his duty only to transmit the information, either from the superior command to the subordinate units or the other way around. That was always the way it was done and it was supposed to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And a third possible situation: The duty operations officer for some -- whatever reason cannot transmit this order to the subordinate unit, can he then go there and convey the commander's order directly? And in that case, what happens with the duty operations officer's post?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As a rule, the duty operations officer should not leave his post. In that case, he would find other ways, either by a different means of communications or by career, to transmit the order. It rarely happens that the duty operations officer would go himself to directly transmit such an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If he did have to go and convey that himself, did somebody then stay to perform the duty of the operations officer?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The post can only be left only with the permission of the commander or the chief of staff. He can go personally himself, but in that case there would be his assistant or another person authorised to perform the duty of an operations officer in his stead.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bojanovic, it states here: "Received and dispatched information." Is the duty operations officer obliged to provide the commander or the chief of staff with the return information, whether he acted upon his orders and whether the instructions were implemented?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If he receives such a message, he is obliged to inform the commander. But if he does not receive it, then he's not obliged to do that. Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. We'll go more slowly. When the duty operations officer carries out the task given to him by the commander and conveys this order, is he obliged, according to the rules, to inform the commander to tell him, I acted on your request or instructions. I have carried out this, I have transmitted the order?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the commander has to be informed that the task was carried out, that the message was transmitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that the commander must be informed about whether the tasks -- task assigned to the duty operations officer was carried out or not?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The commander has to be informed about whether his order had been implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During those days the commander was absent from the Zvornik Brigade and occasionally the chief of staff would also be absent. He would be on the field. Was the commander then in command of the unit via radio communication, even though he wasn't physically present there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The commander, chief of staff, or deputy commander, they all have various means of communication at their disposal and they can use them even though they're not physically present at the headquarters. But they are still in the area of defence of the brigade and they are still in command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that he can be in command even though he's not physically present at the headquarters but is actually in the area of defence of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because he still has means of communication at his disposal. He can use courier service and he can still be in command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We had occasion here to hear the term "the continuity of command." We heard it in the evidence of Mr. Butler. Can you please explain how you understand this concept.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This means that in the brigade, in any unit, there always has to be somebody in command in the area of defence, for example, of the Zvornik Brigade. So if the commander is absent, there should be chief of staff there. If the chief of staff is not there, which happened very rarely, then if it was only a short absence, the chief of staff would appoint assistant for operations and training to be in command at the headquarters. It was very seldom. I don't even remember those occasions that both the chief of staff and commander were absent at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And we come to the key question here: Can duty operations officer at any time be in command of subordinate units, staff units, or battalions?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. He is not there to be in command. He cannot be issuing orders to commanders of battalions and so on. He can only issue orders to his assistant, to couriers, and to technical staff. I as duty operations officer was authorised to tour those standing guard, various guard posts. I could issue orders to my assistant but not to commanders of other units.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At one point today you said that by using means of communication, commander or chief of staff was always able to be in command. What means of communication were available to duty operations officer? Can you please tell us that.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The duty operations officer had so-called local telephone, direct telephone line where we can receive incoming calls from the town. There also was a PTT telephone line. For example, a commander of a battalion who had the so-called civilian telephone line could communicate with commander or chief of staff without informing the duty operations officer about the contents of that conversation. We had so-called many telephone switchboard with four local numbers at the duty operations officer's office, and we used that switchboard to transfer the calls either to commander chief of staff or assistant for logistics. Could the monitor be removed from here, because I can't follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Which means of communication were available for regular communication for the duty operations officer?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Those were most telephones, either field telephones or direct telephone lines or the ones with extensions. And they could also transfer any incoming calls to radio communication. If there were only short distances involved, then courier service could be used as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we give an example. Commander of the Drina Corps or somebody from the headquarters of the Drina Corps calls the brigade and needs to speak to the duty operations officer to convey an order or a request. How would that communication be established? Would it go directly to the duty operations officer or through somebody else?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they could call duty operations officer directly if there was a civilian telephone available. It could also go through a communications centre. They could call the number or a certain extension and say, We need to speak to somebody from the Drina Corps, and then they would connect the line with me through this many switchboard.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The radio communication, did it go through hard wire or through airwaves?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I have to tell you that I'm not an expert in this area, but I think that airwaves were used because we had codes, which must mean that airwaves were used.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During this shift of the duty operations officer, would he occasionally receive a message from the corps without speaking directly to the people in the corps, but rather by receiving it through the radio centre, the communications centre?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that would happen occasionally. We would get a message from the communications centre saying, Well, such-and-such called and they want you to do this and that. But in most cases they would connect us. They would connect the duty operations officer to the person at the headquarters of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Then we have the following situation: Somebody from the corps wishes to transmit a message to the security organ of the Zvornik Brigade. For example, that Beara would arrive the following day at 1500 hours. In that system of message transmitting, what is the role of the duty operations officer?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the duty operations officer would simply have to transmit the message. He would not get involved into the reasons for Beara's visit and so on. He would simply convey the message that Beara would be arriving at such-and-such a time, and that would be the end of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And let us conclude with this topic. If the message doesn't -- is not coming from the commander or the chief of staff of the Zvornik Brigade but rather from the headquarters or the officers at the headquarters of the Drina Corps, would the duty operations officer be authorised or would he be duty-bound to inquire into the reasons why the message is being sent?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, he wouldn't have authority to do that. He would be afraid of inquiring into the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bojanovic. I would like to turn to another area that has to do with the duties of the duty operations officer. You are an operations officer or you are an officer in the morale organ and you take over your 24-hour shift as duty operations officer. So during your shift as duty operations officer, would you still continue to carry out your other duties in your other post?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As soon as somebody takes over the shift of the duty operations officer, all his other duties in the organ where he has his main post are discontinued. So there is a 24-hour stay in carrying out his other regular duties. They are discontinued for that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that during that 24-hour shift he does not continue carrying out his functional duties?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. He does not continue carrying them out. And let me just tell you that the duties of the duty operations officer are so demanding that no one would be able to carry out two different types of duties simultaneously. Therefore, his other regular duties are, so to speak, frozen for a 24-hour period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that that is yet another reason why security organ officer cannot at the same time perform duties of the duty operations officer?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in view of the nature of their work and the peculiarities of their work, they were never appointed to duty operations officer duties. They could not simultaneously carry out the duties of the duty operations officer and the sensitive tasks that they have to carry out as officers of security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you what documents, what notebooks or logbooks, are kept by the duty operations officer.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Regular practice was to have the duty operations officer record any incoming information. This was recorded in the notebook of the duty operations officer. In addition to that, duty operations officer would draft a regular and interim -- or rather, daily and interim combat reports and also record any incoming telegrams.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What is this notebook of the duty operations officer?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The notebook at the brigade was just an ordinary notebook where duty operations officer would record incoming messages, either those coming from civilians, for example, if there were any messages from girlfriends coming in and so on, all of these messages would be recorded so they could be later transmitted on. Also, messages coming in from the commands or messages being sent out to superior commands, requests for materiel, and so on, all of that would be recorded in that notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What about the war logbook?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The war logbook was kept by the operations department. The contents of the war logbook were typically dictated by the assistant chief for operations. He would normally dictate that to one of the officers who had nice handwriting, because there was a record that would be kept for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you about these specifics. You said that the war logbook was a long-term document. What about the notebook of the duty operations officer?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the notebook could be thrown away after it was completed, or it could be put in the archives. So it's not an official document meant to be kept for a long period of time. Sometimes the duty operations officer would scribble in the notebook, whereas the war logbook was not that type of a document, it was an official document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that sometimes officers would write in the notebook information that was not significant in the military sense?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Sometimes that would happen. For example, some civilians would call in and say, Please contact such-and-such and tell them that we want to meet at such-and-such time and so on. So this was basically a record of communication that was coming in. Some information was of a serious nature and some wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that duty operations officer prepared daily and interim combat reports. What does that entail?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: These daily reports at the time were sent every day in the afternoon hours. The duty officer would record what was going on during the day, at the front line, would also record any requests to the superior command, and so on. Sometimes the commander or the chief of staff would be present as the duty officer compiled the daily report. Sometimes they would even dictate it to the duty officer. So these were reports that were sent on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the usher to assist us in order to give the witness an exhibit, P519, which is a daily combat report compiled on the 14th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bojanovic, we have heard here that Mr. Jokic on the 14th to the 15th of July was the duty operations officer, and we had opportunity to see the document that you have in front of you now. I wanted to analyse this document with you now. Does this document have all of the elements that you described to us?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Normally there would be eight, nine, or ten points in combat report. It would describe the situation on the field, the battle front, the -- it described any problems with morale, security. There would also be requests of our units addressed to the Drina Corps. So this is what was contained, and this is just a typical daily combat report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is this report a document of command?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And this is a document meant to inform the superior command on the state of affairs in the area of defence of the Zvornik Brigade. Yes, this is naturally a document which is considered an act of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who signed this document?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Chief of staff, Major Dragan Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could such a daily combat report be sent to the Drina Corps command without the approval, without the knowledge, or without the signature of the chief of staff, Major Dragan Obrenovic at the time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No way that this could happen. The duty operations officer could prepare the daily combat report, but without the signature or approval of the chief of staff it could not be sent to the command. A ready-made report could sometimes lie there for a long time before the chief of staff would come to sign it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You can see here in the left bottom corner, initials DJ/MV.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Since this is the 14th of July when Dragan Jokic was the duty operations officer, what do these initials mean?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: They mean that the report was prepared by Dragan Jokic and it was typed out on the computer by Misko Vasic or somebody else with the same initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What does it mean it was prepared by Dragan Jokic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It means that he processed all the incoming information and requests and entered them into the report point by point. But whoever prepared the report, it couldn't be sent without the appropriate signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does the commander reserve the right to make some entries himself or make corrections in the report previously made?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. He can make corrections or additions that he deems necessary. Because the entire contents of the daily combat report is the responsibility ultimately of the chief of staff or whoever signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me just draw your attention to item 4 of this document. It says: "No extraordinary developments." Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would, for instance, a mass execution or a killing of a large number of prisoners in the zone of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade qualify as an extraordinary event that would have to be reflected in the report and notified to the superior command?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It is an extremely extraordinary event, and it would certainly find its way into the daily combat report intended for the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We know that in the afternoon, in the evening of the 14th of July this event took place. Will you please look at the stamp and tell us when this document was sent to the Drina Corps, at what time, if you can discern it.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see at 1840 hours, if I am reading this correctly. Yes, 1840 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it written in the stamp that it's the 14th of July, or is it a different date?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: 14th of July, but I would say with a question mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Which year?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: 1995 or maybe this digit is actually a 7. Poorly legible in this copy. I don't know why somebody would put the question mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the assistance of the usher, I would like us to look at another document. It is Prosecution Exhibit P120, Your Honours, another document introduced through Mr. Butler. It is an extraordinary combat report of the 14th of July, 1995. Or perhaps the proper translation is interim combat report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It is poorly legible, so I will read it to avoid misunderstanding. Will you please look at it, and if we are unable to read something, we'll try together. Tell me first, what is the date of the report?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: 14th July, 1995. And I can see the date and the month. The year is less -- well, legible. It says "interim report."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please tell us: What is the difference between a daily and an interim report? Is there any difference to the work of the duty operations officer?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The difference is that daily reports were sent every day. Interim reports were only sent in extraordinary situations such as the appearance of large columns, traffic, accidents, or other casualties that would merit an interim report. So apart from regular daily reports, interim reports would be sent only occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Intensive or heavy fighting or large needs that need to be met, would they also qualify as extraordinary events?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What qualifies as an ordinary event is something that could jeopardise the safety of Zvornik town or the Zvornik Brigade, such as a large number of troops of the enemy would be such a danger to the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who signed this interim report, who sent it.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was sent and signed by the chief of staff, Major Dragan Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could an interim report be sent to the Drina Corps command only by the duty operations officer alone, without the signature of the chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The same applies as to the daily report. The duty operations officer would sometimes completely ignore such extraordinary events, and the chief of staff would dictate such an interim report to him and order him to send it to the superior command, either the chief of staff or the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would or could such an interim report be sent through the radio communications centre only signed by the duty operations officer, without the signature of the commander or chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at this report and tell us the time and the day when it was sent to the Drina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: 15th July 1995 at 0110 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that this document was sent in the night of the 14th of July at 10 past 1.00 a.m.?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was in fact the early morning hours of the 15th of July. That's when it was sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that at that moment the document was not sent without the signature of Dragan Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly, because it couldn't be sent without his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that Dragan Obrenovic was indeed at the command of the Zvornik Brigade in order to be able to sign this?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He had to sign this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: That was a very leading question, Your Honour, on a critical point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Rephrase your question, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I believe, Your Honour, that I in fact received the answer and it's quite sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I will finish with this question. Until 10 past 1.00 a.m. on the 15th of July, could this telegram be sent without the signature of Dragan Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, it couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you assist me once again with these initials, DJ/MV in the left bottom corner.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I will repeat. Dragan Jokic drew up the report and Misko Vasic typed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me now move on to another area and ask you about your own movements so that we can relate you to the events concerning Dragan Jokic. If you remember on the 12th of July, the duty officer was Milan Maric.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
