utterances.text: Do you remember where you were on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 13th of July, I was again in the headquarters at the barracks performing various duties upon the orders of Nenad Simic, who was my superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you spend the night of the 14th of July -- sorry, the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The night of the 13th of July, I slept at the headquarters until 2.00 a.m. when I was awakened in order to be given certain tasks that I had to perform.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please tell us what it was all about. What did you do in the night of the 13th of July until the morning of the 14th?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I know that after finishing my daily tasks on the 13th, I was rather tired. However, together with the duty operations officer who was Sreten Milosevic at the time and the chief of staff, I sent a telegram to the command of the Drina Corps. That is one of the events that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember the time, what time it was when you were drawing up this report?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was between 6.00 or maybe 7.00 and 8.00 p.m., I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What happened later?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't feeling very well personally, if you're asking about my movements. So I went to see a doctor at the infirmary. I started sweating all of a sudden. He took my blood pressure, which turned out to be high. It was something like 120 over 170 -- over 70, correction. So I went to get some rest and some sleep. The chief of staff was informed that I was feeling unwell.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened then?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: After that a messenger woke me up and told me that the chief was waiting for me in the duty operations officer room. I got dressed very quickly and went to see him, feeling still drowsy and weak.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see the chief?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, both the previous evening and early in the morning when he was giving me those orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And that happened in the room of the duty operations officer?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And what were the orders?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Although I was feeling unwell, as I said, he ordered me to take a part of our forces, one reinforced platoon strong plus two Pragas - Praga being an anti-aircraft, two-barrelled weapon, 30 millimetre in calibre - plus one Doboj MUP platoon and go to the area of Maricici, a village which is 7 to 10 kilometres away from Zvornik. He told me to leave a part of our forces there in Maricici and take a platoon of the civilian police -- sorry, a company of the civilian police commanded by Captain Zoran Jankovic and link up with the forces taken by then-Captain Maric to the area of Snagovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher assist us at this point, please, so that we can move quickly through this, to show the witness an excerpt from the map that we used yesterday, Your Honours, marked for identification. It was a Defence exhibit, D128.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bojanovic, if you would kindly look at this map and take the pointer to show us where Zvornik is, where you were in the night of the 13th of July, and where you were supposed to go upon Obrenovic's orders as well as the location where you were supposed to link up with the said units.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I left from the barracks in Karakaj with the mentioned units. I passed through Zvornik. I came to the sector of Zlatne Vode. And then I took the Mahmutici road where I arrived at the Maricici sector. That is where I left some of the forces and with the rest I went towards the Snagovo sector where I was supposed to meet up with Captain Maric.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Why did you receive such an order from Obrenovic? Why were you supposed to go to that sector in particular?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That sector was empty. There were no forces of ours there. Based on the interim report and the information about the situation, a large number of Muslims were going toward Tuzla. There was civilians in that column, but about 30 to 40 per cent of the people in the column were armed. So there was a possibility that they would go into Zvornik, which would cause a panic for sure and make the civilian population in Zvornik flee. Srebrenica would be a small -- was a small success in comparison to the fall of Zvornik, because that would be a central point leading to Semberija. That is why we had to disperse or deploy our forces over a broader area in order to prevent such a breakthrough.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At one point you said that members of the police went with you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was a unit that was attached for our assistance. The unit came from Doboj and I've told you who the commander was of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was this the person who the next night on the 14th, in the evening, was captured by the column of the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. When we met up with Major Maric -- actually Captain Maric, I had a different task. This was in the early morning on the 14th. I informed Captain Maric with this other captain. And afterwards I found out that after I left for this other task, that that captain was captured, the commander of the military police unit from the Doboj MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When Obrenovic issued this order to you, did he go with you or did he remain in the command of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know where he was. I left with the units. So I don't know where he was after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you receive this order from Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 14th at 2.00 a.m. in the office of the duty operations officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was he present?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No one else could have issued an order like that except for him, to take these units in the late evening. I had to carry out that order, even though I wasn't feeling so well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, you did not answer the question put to you by the counsel. I would like to hear a direct answer from you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what this is about. Of course I will try to give you a direct answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I will repeat this question. At the time when he issued the order, was Obrenovic personally present in the command of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: He was personally present at the command at 2.00 a.m. on the 14th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Ljubo, can we continue? When did you return to the command of the Zvornik Brigade? What time was that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly what time it was, but as soon as I met up with Maric and handed the company over to him, I took a vehicle, a Peugeot from the command, and returned to the barracks at approximately 6.00 a.m. on the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And what did you do after that in the Zvornik barracks?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember. There was some things to do probably relating to the burial of our forces and probably Major Simic issued some specific tasks. In the meantime --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Just allow me for a second to ask you this: Do you recall the 11th, 12th, and the 13th, and do you remember if you saw Dragan Jokic at all in the Zvornik Brigade command? Did you have any contact with him?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I do not recall seeing him there or having any contacts with him. Had I had any contacts, I'm sure I would remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 14th, according to the information that we have, Dragan Jokic took over as duty operations officer. Do you remember if you had any contacts or activities with him on that day, the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was in the barracks. I probably was doing something regarding the assignments that were ongoing and something that had to do with a task that I was scheduled to carry out on the 15th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would ask you the following: Who was in command? Who was your commander at that point in time? As an officer, under whose command were you? Who was issuing instructions for your work and did that have anything to do with the duty operations officer's tasks?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was under the command of Major Simic as far as my duty operations officer were concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, what's the problem, Ms. Issa?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. I'm just wondering if we can maybe break that up. It just -- there seems to be several questions there and I'm just think perhaps we can streamline it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. It was a compound question. We can go at it one by one. You may proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bojanovic, let us break this up into two questions. First, that day, on the 14th and the 15th, who did you receive your orders from?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's like this -- it's complicated. First I was subordinated to the assistant commander for morale Major Nenad Simic, and I received my tasks from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And Major Nenad Simic, who did he receive his orders from during those days?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Those few days until the return of Commander Pandurevic, he received his orders exclusively from the chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did either of you on those days, the 14th and the 15th of July, receive any kind of orders from the duty operations officer, Dragan Jokic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't receive orders from him. But there was some duties that were established prior to that which I had to carry out on the 15th in cooperation with the duty operations officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us a little bit more about that.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Our unit, our brigade, was helping out in Sekovici. This is a settlement about 40 kilometres from Zvornik and each shift of those people took place on the 15th or the 30th. The people who were helping out would be replaced by a new shift. So that on the 15th, it was my task to implement this shift, to take the new people to their location and bring the ones who were there back to the barracks. So my work with the duty operations officer were as follows: He was supposed to check whether the people who were supposed to go on this new shift, whether they were ready, so that on the 15th, the next day, I could go with him so that we could carry out this takeover.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could the operations officer order you to take or not to take this shift to that location?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. This order was given to me before by the chief of staff. I remember - perhaps this is important to mention - that either over the phone or via radio we talked, not on the 15th. But he told me to pay attention to the sector of Bijela or Zuta Zemlja, which is on the Zvornik/Sekovici road because there was a possibility that the column would break through in that sector. There was also the possibility that a bus could be captured or destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that it was in the record. Who told you this?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This is what the chief of staff told me. He personally told me in his own voice from somewhere out in the field. He said: Pay attention to the Zuta Zemlja or Bijela Zemlja sector. I cannot remember which one it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So you are talking about the 15th in the morning?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, when I was supposed to leave to carry out my assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, I would like to clarify a certain technical problem. Did you provide a statement to the Prosecution before your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I was summoned. It was signed by Mr. Blewitt to appear on the 18th of September, 2001, I think, at the premises of the Tribunal in Banja Luka. I did respond to this call and I provided an interview, as they call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember saying on that occasion that this group that was going to Snagovo and Maricici that you took that group on the 15th in the morning there and not on the 14th in the morning there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember stating that, but I wasn't sure. I got my dates mixed up. I wasn't able to prepare for this interview because all the relevant documents which I could have used to prepare were removed by someone. Later it turned out that this was Lieutenant Colonel Obrenovic who did that. So I made a mistake in the date by a day or two dates and perhaps also in the exact time. So now I am asking the Chamber to forgive me if I got my dates mixed up because it has been ten years almost since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: But you remember at one point investigator Dean Manning asked you whether there was a possibility that this assignment to meet up with Maric was given to you on the 14th in the morning and not on the 15th in the morning. And you said -- as far as you recalled, you said: As far as I remember I am sure it was.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I said that I was sure that it was on the 15th. But later when I looked at the notes which are important, I determined that this was on the 14th in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say by looking at the notes, which notes do you mean?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm thinking about the notes made by the duty operations officer which were not accessible to us who had these interviews with the investigators of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you have access to them? Who had removed them?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot say for certain but later I heard that these books were removed and copied by the chief of staff, Dragan Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you looked at these notes, did that help you to determine the exact date when you went to Snagovo and Maricici?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Once I looked at the book I was then sure about the dates and all the other events that I talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am sorry for exceeding the time, but I think that this is a good opportunity to go on our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stojanovic, are you going to finish your direct examination today or we have to continue tomorrow morning for your direct?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am really sincerely hoping, Your Honours, that we will finish today. We still have two documents to look at and the notebook of the duty operations officer, so I think that I will not run into a time problem. But in any case, I thank you for your patience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it seems to me that of course the testimony of this witness is relevant to your client, but however I see there are very few possibility of disputes concerning this testimony. I just hope you bear that in mind and try to streamline your questions. You may proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bojanovic, if you remember, we stopped before the break on the 15th of July when you were leaving with this shift. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us briefly where you went on the 15th of July.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The officer on duty or his career woke me up at 5.00 a.m. so that I would have enough time to prepare to take the shift to Sekovici. The shift assembled around 9.00 a.m. I took them all in a bus where the handover of the shift took place. I came in the afternoon between 1500 hours and 1530 hours, and somebody told me that I should go to Kitovnice to the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I just have a question for you about the forward command post. Could you please tell us about that.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The IKM, "Isturevo komandno mesto," is a forward command post. It was located in Kitovnice and that post is used in emergency situations or in the course of combat operations, which is what the situation was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And what happens at the IKM, who is there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Almost all members of the inner command are at the IKM, the chief of staff. If the commander is present, he is there, too. So the main focus of the activities of the command is transferred to the IKM.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And are duty operations shifts organised at the IKM?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They are organised there the same way that they're organised in the command post. And sometimes a duty operations officer has more work there and his duties are increased in comparison to the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that in July during intense combat operations, there was also duty operations service established at the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you: Was there a notebook of the duty operations officer at the forward command post as well?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember that because at the time I didn't serve as duty operations officer at the forward command post. But I assume that some notes were taken and also daily combat reports and interim combat reports were sent to the superior command. Therefore, I believe that there was some kind of record there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean on the 15th at the forward command post there was also a person on duty as duty operations officer?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, just like in the days prior to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps this would be the right time to ask you whether you know the code name for the duty operations officer at the Zvornik Brigade command?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the barracks, the code name was Palma and at the forward command post the code name was Palma II, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, Palma II was the code name for the forward command post. That was the call sign?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Upon your return to the headquarters of the Zvornik Brigade in the afternoon on the 15th, where did you go from there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I received an order from some senior officer to report to the forward command post in Kitovnice. Therefore, I drove in a vehicle to the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it possible that on the 15th of July, you were the duty operations officer at the headquarters of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. That's out of question. I could not have been both in charge of the shift, taking the shift to their location, be the duty operations officer, and be present at the forward command post all at the same time. That's impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When did you arrive at the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I arrived at the forward command post at around 1700 hours or 1730, perhaps even a bit later because it took me some time to change my clothing, take some rest, and only after that did I go with the driver to the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How far is it to the forward command post from the headquarters of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't give you the accurate number, but between 15 and 20 kilometres from Karakaj where the headquarters of the brigade was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How long did it take you to cover that distance from the command of the Zvornik Brigade to the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I think between 45 minutes and one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was it a macadam road?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. The driver was the one who drove, and I can't remember whether we went via Orahovac or Jardan, but I know that -- I know what time it was approximately when I reached the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: For the sake of the record, what is the name of that other place. Was it Jardan?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Jardan, with an R.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who did you find at the forward command post?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: There definitely was the commander there, Vinko Pandurevic, because it was evening already and he had returned from the forces from the Srebrenica sector. I think that I also saw assistant commander for security there as well as assistant chief of staff for communications. Also present was the officer for intelligence and reconnaissance information, Mica Petkovic. I'm not quite positive about him. That was the first time that I saw Commander Pandurevic, following his departure to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive orders from Pandurevic at that time or from Obrenovic? Who was in command of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When the commander is present, then he is in charge, meaning Commander Pandurevic. But I also could have received orders from the chief of staff and the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where is the forward command post? What does it represent? What kind of a facility is it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This is the weekend house, a small one, prefabricated, where they had a small kitchen, one or two rooms, and that was the forward command post; whereas, the observation post was in Kitovnice a little further away.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you: On the 15th in the afternoon when you came to the headquarters of the Zvornik Brigade, did you see Dragan Jokic there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see him there. I didn't see him at the brigade upon my return from Sekovici, nor did I see him at the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: From the forward command post, could one communicate, and by what means, with the Drina Corps or with the brigade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was possible to communicate, both with the brigade and the corps command. With the brigade we had a telephone line, meaning that directly through the communications centre one could contact the command of the Drina Corps. And there was also a signalman on duty with RUP-12 equipment, which was used to establish connection.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the forward command post also have means of communication with the battalion?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure about that. There probably was something. I don't know whether their communication went through the duty operations officer or there was a direct line, which I doubt. It was most likely that through the duty operations officer at the barracks they had communication with all battalions. They could also communicate with them via the radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember on that afternoon of the 15th anything particular about your activities?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I remember seeing Commander Pandurevic then, chief of staff appeared later. They talked in the weekend house. I wasn't present there. They talked for 30 minutes to 45 minutes. What was important for me was that after their conversation, I was asked to come to the weekend house, the command post. I was asked to come in, and he dictated an interim combat report to me, which was to be sent to the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: For the sake of the record, tell us please who asked you to go into the weekend house and dictated the interim combat report to you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was Commander Pandurevic. I was one of the officers with good handwriting, so he wanted to make sure that it would be legible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please assist us in presenting the next exhibit to the witness, which is Exhibit P528. This is a document tendered during the evidence of Mr. Richard Butler. This is interim combat report dated 15th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bojanovic, you have now in front of you a handwritten interim combat report. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is this your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is definitely my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at the heading. On what date was this report compiled?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The 15th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who was it sent to?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Interim combat report was sent from the brigade, just like daily combat reports, to the Drina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at the second page and tell us who signed this report. Whose report is this?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Vinko Pandurevic. The commander signed the document. It's not a full signature; he just initialled it. But this is definitely his handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Looking at the form and the contents of this report, is it identical to the other ones that you described before?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They are all the same, regardless of where they are sent from. Both interim and daily combat reports have the same contents. They are approved and sent either by the commander or the chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So this report couldn't be sent to the Drina Corps command without a signature of the commander or chief of staff either?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Regardless of whether the report is sent from the forward command post or the main command post, the commander who was present had to sign it, either the commander or the chief of staff who was standing in if the commander was absent. Nobody else could have signed these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it possible that you wrote this report when you were quite at a distance from Vinko Pandurevic and when he dictated this to you via the radio?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, that would have been impossible. I sat down, took two sheets of paper, and he dictated this report to me. We had no typewriter there. And as I was considered to have good handwriting, I was asked to do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would it be possible, hypothetically, to have this dictated via telephone or via radio connection and then sent without a signature?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. That would be impossible. Somebody always had to sign the report before it was sent to the superior command, because one never knows who is on the other side of the line and who is dictating the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you sure that this is Vinko Pandurevic's signature?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm 100 per cent certain. First he signed the report in my presence, and, second, I know both his initials and his full signature. I'm well acquainted with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stojanovic, I think you have already exhausted the questions on that very issue. The witness's answer is quite certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will just read out the bit that has most relevance in this telegram. This is precisely why I was putting these questions. If you remember, we heard that Obrenovic also dictated the interim combat report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, Mr. Bojanovic, could you please read out slowly the second and the third paragraph of the text of this interim combat report.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Should I start here where it says "additional burden"?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: "An additional burden for us is the large number of prisoners distributed throughout schools in the brigade area, as well as the duties pertaining to security and sanitisation of the terrain." The next paragraph: "This command cannot take care of these problems any longer, as it has neither the materiel or other resources needed. In no one else takes over this responsibility, I will be forced to release them."

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On that occasion, as you were writing out this text, did you learn anything from Pandurevic about the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: All I learned was what I wrote down. To tell you the truth, I'm like a typist typing what somebody else is dictating. So I didn't inquire about anything because we were in a difficult situation. So I didn't inquire anything -- about anything outside of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This information about the prisoners, did he write it down before or after his conversation with Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I told you it was after their conversation which lasted 45 minutes to one hour. So after that he called me in and dictated this to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please read out what it says on the stamp. When was this sent to the Drina Corps command?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The 15th of July, 1995, at 19.25.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How long does it take to send this telegram after you have finished writing it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The telegram can be sent right away, because at the forward command post there is a duty signalman who can transmit the encoded report to the Drina Corps command. You can see right away that this was sent by a different signalman, the one who was present at the forward command post, not the one who was at the main command post in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we now go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those are precisely the pages. Go to the place where it says "16th of July." Can you recognise whose handwriting that is and does that resemble your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you right away that I always use the Cyrillic script and I don't see any Cyrillic script here or any handwriting that would resemble mine. The other handwritings, I don't know. 16th, I don't know. It depends who was the duty operations officer. If I knew who that was, perhaps then I could tell whether that was their handwriting or not. But in any case, there is -- my handwriting is not here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Any of the other people who were duty operations officers in the Zvornik Brigade and were working in the same tasks that you worked at, did any of them use the Cyrillic script? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I cannot. I remember that the late Captain Momo Vasiljevic, who happened to be a relative of mine, also used the Cyrillic script. Such people who used the Cyrillic script were rare, there were perhaps three or four of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bojanovic. Could you please tell us what was happening on the night of the 15th and where you were on the 16th, but let's go step by step. Where were you on the night of the 15th to the 16th?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When I wrote this report which was sent, I, just like a majority of the officers who were thinking maturely in that situation, attempted to remove myself from those officers and from the chief. Because, like I said, in that situation I could have been given a kind of assignment which would have put my in jeopardy. So that is why I pulled back to the command of the 4th Battalion and spent the night there. In the morning, I reported to the IKM, and then afterwards I went to the Zvornik barracks again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you at the Zvornik barracks on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, on the 16th --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may ask for us to move into private session again for a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now we are in open session. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bojanovic, at one point you said on the night of the 15th because of being in jeopardy you decided to move out of the command. What did you mean when you said that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, our lines were threatened from the front and from the rear. And it could have happened that I had to go to help somebody out. This was a dangerous situation, so it was normal for me to put myself out of harm's way so I would not be jeopardised. So I went a couple of kilometres away from the forward command post simply to get lost so I wouldn't be seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what your duties were on that day, on the 16th in the command of the Zvornik Brigade? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember, but it was probably something to do with my organ for morale. And I know that I received an oral order from the commander for the next day, the 17th, since we didn't see each other to go to the IKM and to go and search the terrain in a certain sector. And perhaps I will tell you where I was supposed to go. Together with the assistant chief of staff for operations and a company from the 16th Krajina Motorised Brigade, I was supposed to go to search the terrain, and I did that. In the following -- along the following axis: IKM, Baljkovica, Kisla [phoen], elevation 602, and Crni Vrh. That was the axis. To sweep the terrain, to make sure that there were no killed or wounded of ours and also to make sure that there were no enemy soldiers like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: While you were searching the terrain on the 17th, did you encounter enemy soldiers and did you have any clashes with them?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The group that we were taking, the group being taken by Major Dragutinovic and myself, this unit from Banja Luka, did not encounter any enemy troops. But we found two dead soldiers of ours at Baljkovica. One of them was lying along the road. I happen to know one of them, his name was Mrda. He was a member of the sabotage reconnaissance detachment. We did not find any other bodies or fighters from our side or from the enemy's side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us which units were sweeping the terrain on the 17th.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This company-sized unit was led by a major. I cannot remember his name. It came as reinforcement in this emergency situation. But since they didn't know the terrain very well, then the assistant chief of staff and I went to take them through this terrain which we were familiar with. We swept the terrain again on the 18th and the 19th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was there any fighting on the 18th or the 19th? Were any members of the BiH Army captured?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In that section where my assignment was, there was no fighting. Because the main part of those forces -- of their forces had already crossed over into their terrain. There were some breakthroughs, so that -- through the territory, so that I, myself, and my unit did not have any encounters with the enemy troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any other groups who were also sweeping the terrain on orders of the command of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this was only one section that we were covering. There were other sections, both in the rear of the zone of defence of the brigade and especially in places where the line of defence was broken through. I don't know what their sectors were, but I'm sure that there were other units who were performing the same tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 17th, 18th, or the 19th of July, did you meet Dragan Jokic anywhere, in the command of the Zvornik Brigade or anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't have that opportunity. I was in the woods with that unit, so there was no opportunity for me to see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bojanovic, throughout these few days from the 12th, 13th, up until the 20th of July, did you have the opportunity to see security officers of the Drina Corps or from the Main Staff or any other officers from the superior command in the Zvornik Brigade command?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: There were such officers, probably ones from the Drina Corps and from the Main Staff. I didn't know them. And when I was in my office on duty, they didn't address me. I didn't have any contacts with them. But there were some officers whom I didn't know. I know Colonel Beara, but I didn't see him at that time. I don't know about the others. I don't know who they were, whether they were from the security organ or other departments. In any case, I didn't have any contacts with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you notice what they were doing, what was the reason for their presence in the Zvornik Brigade command or in that area in general?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I thought it was because of this emergency situation with the arrival and passage of the column, so I believed that it was their task to provide moral and other kinds of support in this difficult situation. But I don't know exactly what they did. I also don't know who they were in contact with.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you find out later that parallel with these legal and legitimate operations, there was also the dramatic situation with the executions?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I was at the barracks doing my job, and I only found out about it from the media after the signing of the Dayton Accords. There was talk around town, but I didn't have the opportunity to check anything. In any case, at the brigade command after those events and in particular during these events which were proved to have happened, there was no word about it, it wasn't discussed, it wasn't analysed, there were no meetings about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bojanovic, as one of the most experienced officers there, at least in your years of work, what is your comment on that, on the fact that such an important event was never analysed at an official meeting and that this question was never dealt with in the command of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's my opinion that certain officers really did not know about it. Some officers knew about it from the civilian authorities and the security organs. And this was not accessible to us, this information I mean. And it's a good thing that it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was this shame being concealed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, most probably. Everybody was ashamed of such a shameful act, and quite rightly so. Besides the officers who participated in this, there are many honest men who wouldn't even think of doing such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please allow me to go through some documents in which your name is mentioned and then you can help us to go through them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please show the witness the relevant pages from the duty operations officer's notebook in which the name of Ljubo Bojanovic is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bojanovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, these are exhibits P507, ERN number 03089342, and B/C/S version ERN number 02935747.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bojanovic, please take a look. This page is dated the 14th of July, and for your information Dragan Jokic was the duty operations officer at the brigade command. It says here: "Dubravka called Ljubo Bojanovic."

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain this?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Dubravka is not a code name of any organ or any senior officer. This is a girl who lived in my mother's house and was dating the driver of Commander Pandurevic. And since she knew me, she would call me to convey a message. And this is an example of one of those messages of nonserious nature that I described to you earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise the handwriting of Dragan Jokic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If he was the duty operations officer, he would do this in a proper way. I can't remember now, but that's probably how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Why is it that Dubravka, the girlfriend of the driver, contacted you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Because she knew me. She didn't know Jokic, so she couldn't have conveyed a message through Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now turn to another relevant page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is again Exhibit P507, ERN 03089348, the English version. And the B/C/S version 02935753.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Again, these are notes taken while Dragan Jokic was the duty operations officer, and here underneath the 15th of July it says here: "Wake up Milosevic" at 6.15. "Ljubo" at 5.50. Can you explain what this means?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this was the 15th of July and I had to take people to their shifts. So I had to get up early in the morning, get ready, see whether the unit was ready, to see whether they had the necessary materiel and the equipment. So I had to get up a bit earlier, although this is not very early. But I had to do this in order to prepare.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that assistant commander for logistics, Sreten Milosevic, also slept at the headquarters of the brigade and had to be awakened at 6.15?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, definitely. Because had he been at home, there would have been a civilian telephone number here, through which the assistant duty officer or duty operations officer would call him to wake him up. So this means that he was in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let us turn to another relevant page where the name of today's witness is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this again is exhibit P507. The relevant page in English is ERN number 03089366 and B/C/S version is ERN number 02935771.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bojanovic, these are the notes of the duty operations officer on the 16th of July, where it says: "The vehicle from Banja Luka of the company station is to be sent to the school in Orahovac once it arrives," reported by Ljubo Bojanovic at a certain hour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bojanovic, would you please explain to us what this note is about.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me say first that this is not in my handwriting. And once again this proves on the 16th I was in the barracks and somebody gave me this information. Most likely this had to do with the fact that this company of the 16th Motorised Brigade arrived in a certain area, and that the vehicle had broken down. So my message was when this vehicle arrives, finally, it should go to the repair workshop. So this is not my handwriting. I don't know who conveyed this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: According to this note, you are reporting that once this vehicle from Banja Luka arrives it should go to the school in Orahovac. So this was a message arriving from somebody?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I conveyed this message, that this vehicle had broken down. And then I reported to the duty operations officer that once the vehicle arrives it should go to Orahovac. And he wrote that down, and this was probably reported to the command and then further on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have just one more relevant page from the notebook of the duty operations officer. This is an exhibit P133, because this notebook is split into two exhibits, ERN number 03089372, the English version. And the B/C/S version is 02935777. Mr. Bojanovic, let us take a look at this. These are the notes of the duty operations officer on the 18th of July. It says here: "The duty officer at the forward command post, Dusko Vukotic, according to the plan, Ljubo Bojanovic is going."

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, between the lines. This means that Dusko Vukotic was supposed to be at the command post and I was to go instead of him to take that company to sweep the terrain. Because at the forward command post we either had the commander or the chief of staff and there was no need to have the duty operations officer there. Therefore, I could have performed other duties at the task. This is not added here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So this note of the duty operations officer, does it reflect the actual message? Was that the message that Ljubo Bojanovic was to go?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the message, that I was to go instead of Dusko Vukotic. And I definitely went and performed those tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean, Mr. Bojanovic, that the duty of the duty operations officer is simply to record what is ordered?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The duty officer couldn't tell me the reasons why I was supposed to go there. He just told me: You have to go there. And it is possible that even I, myself, didn't know the reasons for that until I reached the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us just take a look to see whether your name is mentioned in intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For your sake, Your Honours, this is P295, A and B, from the collection of intercepts near Sanac [as interpreted] and Konoj [phoen] -- near Okresanica and Konoj.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bojanovic, according to the information received from the OTP and based on the testimony of witnesses who testified here, on the 24th of July, 1995, there was a conversation taking place which was intercepted. So on the 24th of July at 0640 hours, the participants of this conversation were General Krstic and Major Bojanovic, the duty officer. This is how the conversation transpired: "Krstic: Is everything all right?" "Bojanovic: Well, there were some attacks last night on the road from the back, mainly without casualties. Six Turks were captured. "Krstic: Excellent. Great job. Where are they? "Bojanovic: Hello? "Krstic: Yes, yes. "Bojanovic: We have interruptions. "Krstic: Where are they? "Bojanovic: Well, some of them -- I hear the detention facility's full. There are more than 30 of them." I wanted to ask you, Mr. Bojanovic, do you remember having this conversation?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I know that I was the duty officer on the 23rd and 24th, so it is possible that this was me and it was also possible that this was my assistant because this was taking place at 6.40 in the morning. So it is possible that he was substituting me. But again, I -- it could have been me who was speaking to General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. In that case, let me ask you this: Do you remember that on the 24th there were some prisoners in the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I was reported through communications department that there were some prisoners, that there was six of them. Later on the security organs and military police put them in our detention facility. And we already had some prisoners from before there. They were used for exchanges because the other side had our prisoners. So later on all of them were taken to Batkovici to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bojanovic, were you asked by investigators in Banja Luka about this intercept?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I gave them the same answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion did you also draw a sketch of the location where the prisoners were?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I drew a sketch of the ground floor at the headquarters, the command, where the detention facility was, pursuant to the request of the investigators. I also drew a sketch of the upper floor of the brigade headquarters where the office of the duty operations officer was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please briefly tell us where was the detention facility and where was the office of the duty operations officer.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Based on my sketch one could see that the detention facility was across the hall from the dining room, cafeteria. That facility had in the past been used for our soldiers who had some discipline transgressions or had deserted and so on. And at that time it was used as a detention facility for the prisoners, soldiers, from their forces. From my office, one couldn't see that detention facility. Nobody from the upper floor could see the detention facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Then how come -- how is, Mr. Bojanovic, that you knew that there were over 30 prisoners and that the detention facility was full?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I personally avoided going and seeing the prisoners, but it must be that the commander of the detention facility informed me as the duty operations officer about the number of prisoners. The people from logistics also knew this number because they had to provide the accommodation and the food.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So this was on the 24th of July?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened with these prisoners, do you know?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As I heard later, all of them were taken to Batkovici to be exchanged. I'm not sure; that's what I heard. I wish it were like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bojanovic. I will have just two more questions and then we can conclude. How long did you stay in the army?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: After the combat ceased, after the Dayton Accords were signed, I was able to return to the school. I was offered the position of a principal, but due to the years of service I needed in order to retire, I remained with the Army of Republika Srpska and I kept the rank of major.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Have you left active service?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have. And my pension hasn't been regulated yet. I left service on the 31st of December, 1999, pursuant to the decision of Minister Miluvanovic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Before the war and after the war, did you have any friends who were Muslims?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In my neighbourhood there were mostly Muslims living. I went to school with them, we grew up together, and we had very good relations. We were on very good terms. And when these stupid conflicts arose, I thought that all of it would be over in 10 to 15 days. I had no idea it would go on for four years. I had very many Muslim friends, good friends. Also when I was at the military academy, I had many friends who were Muslims or Albanians. We in Zvornik grew up in a multi-ethnic environment, so we never differentiated between the members of various ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bojanovic, after the war have you heard from your Muslim friends or neighbours, acquaintances, anything negative about Dragan Jokic? I'm asking you this while you're still under oath.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I never heard anything bad about him. There were many nice young men in that neighbourhood, and I saw many of them who knew Jokic. And I never heard from them anything bad about Mr. Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you to be blamed for the fact that Dragan Jokic went to the academy and became a soldier?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, partially I am to be blamed. But he didn't have to follow my advice. When I was at the academy, the rule was that when you went home for leave you had to wear a uniform. So he was able to see me at home in my uniform and always used to comment on how good I looked in that uniform and that this is what prompted him to join the profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bojanovic, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karnavas, do you have any questions to put to this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I think -- I think I might be able to finish within the five-minute period we have left, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Bojanovic, I just have a few questions with respect to Witness 130, that's the individual we have been speaking about in closed session. Okay? So we will be referring to him as 130 because he is protected. Okay?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, according to Witness 130 he states -- he stated to the Prosecution when he gave a statement to them on May 23rd, 2004, that on July 13th, 1995, you were the operation duty officer, and on that particular day you ordered him to escort a convoy to Bratunac. My question is very simple: Is that a truthful comment, truthful statement, from Witness 130?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That is far from the truth. I told you about my activities on the 13th, what I did. So in that case, I couldn't have -- first of all, as a duty operations officer I couldn't issue any orders to him, if that answer is satisfactory to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But on that particular day, July 13th, were you the duty operations officer, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, we're going to go to July 15th. Same witness, Witness 130, again in his statement, May 23rd, 2004, he said that -- and this was -- you were asked about this but I want to go into it in a more concrete fashion. He stated to the Prosecution that you were surprised to see him on that particular day, and that you had asked him: How come you're not with the security organ in Petkovci where they were carrying out executions? Concretely, is this a truthful statement from Witness 130, who is now trying to implicate you of having knowledge of and perhaps even participating in those events?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If you need a more detailed answer, I will repeat what I told the Defence [as interpreted] lawyers. I didn't have any encounters as such because I couldn't have been in two places at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So is it a truthful statement or is Witness 130 being untruthful?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all a witness cannot comment on the veracity of another witness. I don't think that form of the question is proper. And secondly, I think the witness has already answered the question. I don't -- it doesn't need an answer. It doesn't need to be repeated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think the second objection stands. I believe the witness already answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, he stated that on that particular day, July 15, again you were the operation duty officer, although later on in another interview he wasn't quite sure. On that particular day, July 15th, were you the duty operation officer, yes or no, just concretely?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, this question has been asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. I understand. But we're going to hear from Witness 130 and I'm already setting my eye sights on him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, on July 15th, 1995, according to Witness 130, again having told this to the Prosecutors having been questioned on one of the many occasions, indicated that you saw Beara, Colonel Beara speaking with Mr. Jokic. Did you see this? Again, he stated that on that particular day you were also the duty operation officer.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: According to what he said, it turns out that I was on duty every day and that I was in constant contact with the security officers. I think he said what suited him, and I am saying what -- what I am saying is the truth and I am speaking it under oath. I didn't see Colonel Beara, I repeat that, (Redacted) in that period. (Redacted). Now, we also indicated, he also indicated that you passed on an order to him regarding sanitation, an order that -- a conversation that had taken place between you and Mr. Deronjic, who was the head of the SDS in Bratunac. Did this ever occur?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I know Mr. Deronjic only from the trials which were conducted here, but I never saw him in my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But did you have a conversation with Mr. Deronjic about sanitation and then have a conversation with Witness 130, conveying to him information about sanitation, asanacija?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Believe me, I'm shocked by these statements. I don't know Deronjic. I'm not -- asanacija or restoration of the terrain is not something that's in my domain, and I don't know what this witness said. I'm sorry, I'm making mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Just one final question. You were questioned on 18th September, 2001, and the gentleman we've been speaking about has given numerous statements, and this one, the one I'm referring to, was back on the 23rd of May, 2004. My question is very simple: Since the Prosecution learned this information from Witness 130, that is May 2004, have they by any chance visited you or requested to meet with you to go over this information to see whether Witness 130 was providing them with true, accurate, and complete information?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Since the conclusion of the combat operations, no one sought anything other than this request for me to go to Banja Luka to speak to Mr. Manning. Other than that, neither side got in touch with me, because I wouldn't have anything to tell them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, let me be very concrete. Witness 130 as late as May 2004 has implicated you in these atrocities. And my question is: Did anyone from OT -- from the Office of the Prosecution contact you to see whether you would be willing to comment on Witness 130's information? In other words to get the other side of the story, verify?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I repeat once again, none of the Prosecution staff got in touch with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And had they gotten in touch with you, would you have been willing to meet with them and discuss these matters with them?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO BOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Of course I would agree to meet with them, and it would have been good to apply as a witness. It would have probably done some good to Witness 130 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Bojanovic. I appreciate your candor. I have no further questions.
